item.title: Reading Speculations Concerning the First Ultraintelligent Machine
item.description:
In 1964 [1], I. J. Good wrote Speculations Concerning the First Ultraintelligent Machine. I've only ever seen it cited for a single paragraph:

Let an ultraintelligent machine be defined as a machine that can far surpass all the intellectual activities of any man however clever. Since the design of machines is one of these intellectual activities, an ultraintelligent machine could design even better machines; there would then unquestionably be an "intelligence explosion," and the intelligence of man would be left far behind ... Thus the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control. It is curious that this point is made so seldom outside of science fiction. It is sometimes worthwhile to take science fiction seriously.

This is becoming increasingly relevant, with the AI Futures Project now estimating an intelligence explosion starting in 2027 in response to recent AI progress in automating AI research. Making our 'last invention' relinquishes our influence over the future, we have to get it right, and with the current frantic pace disastrous mistakes are likely.

I think the appropriate reaction to this news is something like "this is completely irresponsible, you're way too likely to get us all killed, do not do that" and marching in the streets (hence yesterday's protest attendance). But as someone who is very interested in how people process ideas and what they thought with the information they had at the time, my reaction also includes wanting to know more about what Good expected six decades ago.

I spent this morning reading his paper and talking about it with Claude (Fable 5.2). I was curious how the ideas had held up, what he got right, and what he got wrong. Some of his ideas were very technical, and not being an ML expert I can't add much there; I've put these in a Claude-authored appendix.

The first sentence reads very differently now:

The survival of man depends on the early construction of an ultraintelligent machine.

I think he was saying that he was worried that without one we'd kill ourselves off (later he writes "it will give the human race a good chance of surviving indefinitely"). This was during the Cold War, a couple years after the Cuban Missile Crisis, and before any agreement to limit (let alone reduce) nuclear stockpiles.

But now I'd interpret it the other way around: our survival depends on 'early construction' the same way that a driver's survival depends on how quickly they drive.

Reading further, the most-quoted paragraph still jumps out, and not just through familiarity. Reading it closely, the "provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control" is actually pretty prescient: he's essentially describing the plan of record, as much as there is one. Have AI research how to align AI. (This might work! But it also might not.)

He's also uncertain about whether it will go well. In the famous paragraph above he has a "provided that the machine is docile enough", later he says "the sign is uncertain" (math-speak for "could be good or bad"), and speculates whether "the human race will become redundant". He does seem overall optimistic, though, both in the 'survival depends' quote (above) and a few other places. For example, "the machines will create social problems, but they might also be able to solve them in addition to those that have been created by microbes and men."

A live objection at the time was that there wasn't any reason to make AI, and he cites B. V. Bowden's view that "it is easier to construct human brains by the usual method" before responding:

This shows that highly intelligent people can overlook the "intelligence explosion." It is true that it would be uneconomical to build a machine capable only of ordinary intellectual attainments, but it seems fairly probable that if this could be done then, at double the cost, the machine could exhibit ultraintelligence.

I'd actually count this as a bit of a miss: a machine capable of human-level work that was massively cheaper than humans could still be highly economical, and that's essentially what today's deployment of AI is. I suspect he didn't anticipate the extent to which high throughput would precede high intelligence.

I also don't see where his "double the cost" is coming from, and in practice this jump is likely to be much larger. But the critical thing he gets right is that human-level isn't a ceiling, and in a series of domains (games, coding, cybersecurity, math...) we've seen AI, after spending a while at "toy" and some time at "useful tool", quickly pass "human level" to get to something much more capable. I expect this keeps going.

On the technical side, most of the details are in Claude's appendix but at a high level it seems like he was right about a lot of how we got here. He thought it would be "vast artificial neural circuitry" and expected it would learn from experience and reinforcement:

Yet a detailed knowledge of semantics might not be required, since the artificial neural network will largely take care of it, provided that the parameters are correctly chosen, and provided that the network is adequately integrated with its sensorium and motorium (input and output). For, if these conditions are met, the machine will be able to learn from experience, by means of positive and negative reinforcement, and the instruction of the machine will resemble that of a child.

He also anticipated how text-based this would all be:

Whether a machine of classical or ultraparallel design is to be the first ultraintelligent machine, it will need to be able to handle or to learn to handle ordinary language with great facility. This will be important in order that its instructor should be able to teach it rapidly, and so that later the machine will be able to teach the instructor rapidly. It is very possible also that natural languages, or something analogous to them rather than to formal logic, are an essential ingredient of scientific imagination. Also the machine will be called upon to translate languages, and perhaps to generate fine prose and poetry at high speed, so that, all in all, linguistic facility is at a high premium.

He also correctly anticipated that AIs would use traditional computers (still then in their infancy) as tools, with coding and search:

In any event the ultraintelligent machine might as well have a large electronic computer at its beck and call, and also a multimillion dollar information-retrieval installation of large capacity but of comparatively slow speed, since these would add little to the total cost.

And he anticipated a period before AI fully surpassed humans, during which they'd work together:

Until an ultraintelligent machine is built perhaps the best intellectual feats will be performed by men and machines in very close, sometimes called "symbiotic," relationship

This is how many of us work daily, including both my day job and these blog posts.

He was also a strong chess player (on the Bletchley Chess Club during the war) and suggested:

so-called "randomized chess," in which the positions of the white pieces on the first rank are permuted at random before the game begins (but with the two bishops on squares of opposite colors), and then the initial positions of the black pieces are determined by mirror symmetry. This gives rise to 1440 essentially distinct initial positions and effectively removes from the game the effect of mere parrot learning of the openings

This is very close to Chess960 (though without the extra castling work) which Bobby Fischer proposed decades later, and I was initially pretty excited to see it. But reading more it turns out this was a known variant going back centuries. Good's including it here to illustrate that what we really care about is the reasoning component of chess, not memorizing opening lines.

Thinking about things Good got wrong, the timing initially seems like a big one: "more probable than not ... within the twentieth century". But he only put it at 50%, and while it has taken longer it looks like it's going much faster than most others predicted.

A much larger miss is the cost of artificial neurons:

If we could raise say a hundred billion dollars we might be able to simulate all the neurons of a brain, and of a whole man, at a cost of ten dollars per artificial neuron.

Since Moore's law is newer than Good's writing it's not surprising that he didn't fully account for it (though he did expect "great advances in microminiaturization"), but the hardware to power an artificial neuron costs ~10,000x less than this (~$0.01 in current dollars, less if you quantize; Good's $10 would be ~$100 today).

On the other hand, and more importantly, he's in the right ballpark on total cost: the world has spent maybe $1T to date creating AI systems and I expect we spend maybe that again by the end of 2027 as recursive self-improvement increases the returns to AI R&D. Good's $100B is $1T in current dollars, but note that he didn't expect anyone to pay this:

But it seems unlikely that more than say [$300M then; $3B today] would actually be forthcoming, and even this amount might be difficult to obtain without first building the machine!

This is indeed how funding has worked, with investors putting in more money in response to initial progress. That he ended up close to right on the ~$1T looks to me like less of a coincidence than it appears: costs come down over time, and it's only when they're getting into an economically feasible range that someone might actually do it.

The biggest miss, though, is about focus. He was super early in thinking about whether such a machine would be good for the world, but then spends almost the entire paper on how one might be designed. Focusing on the "how" and not the "whether" is very normal for technical people then and now, and as an engineer I feel this pull as well. But it's something people have been getting wrong since the beginning: excitement about the potential, not staring hard at the true scale of the risk.

This paper isn't the last we have of Good's thinking, however, and in 1998 he provided a bio to the IEEE on receiving their Computer Pioneer Award. It doesn't seem to have been used at the ceremony or published, but James Barrat says Good's assistant Leslie Pendleton gave him a copy, and Barrat quotes it in his 2013 Our Final Invention. Note that this is Good writing about himself in the third person:

"The survival of man depends on the early construction of an ultra-intelligent machine." Those were his words during the Cold War, and he now suspects that "survival" should be replaced by "extinction." He thinks that, because of international competition, we cannot prevent the machines from taking over.

How to get countries to coordinate to prevent the machines from taking over is a key question today.

Appendix: Good's technical predictions I asked Claude Fable 5.2 to write an appendix. The judgments are its own, and I haven't checked them:

Most of Good's paper is a theory of how a neural network could store meaning and recall it. Below I go through its main technical claims and say how well I think each matches how current AI systems work. I grade each as a strong match, a partial match, a loose match, or a miss.

Two cautions first. A 58-page speculative paper makes a lot of claims, and picking out the ones that look right in hindsight flatters it. And Good was less of a lone voice than this list might suggest. Neural networks were an active research area in the early 1960s: he cites Rosenblatt's perceptron work, and builds on Hebb, Ashby, and Shannon. His bet was on one of the two live approaches, the one that then went out of fashion for decades and eventually won.

Learning is adjusting connection strengths. Strong match. In his radio-linked machine (p35, p36):

The strength of the connection could be represented by the accuracy of the tuning. ... "Positive reinforcement" would correspond to improved tuning of these filters.
Every connection has an adjustable strength, and learning means changing the strengths. That is what a "weight" is in a modern network, and training is nothing more than adjusting weights.

How the strengths get adjusted. Miss. Good's rule (p80) is that a connection has a small random chance of stepping up in strength whenever it is "successfully used (i.e., contributes to the activation or inhibition of an artificial neuron)". This is a local rule: each connection changes based only on its own activity. Modern networks are trained by backpropagation, which works out how every weight in the network contributed to an error in the final output and adjusts them all together. Nothing in the paper anticipates this, and local rules of Good's kind have not been made to work at scale.

What "reinforcement" means. Partial match. Jeff asked whether Good's "positive and negative reinforcement" from an instructor is what is now called reinforcement learning from human feedback. It does resemble it, and that technique is used to shape how current models behave. But most of what those models know comes from a different source, predicting the next word across a vast amount of text. Good's usage is broader than reward from an instructor. The rule above involves no instructor, he says the machine is educated only "partly" by reinforcement (p80), and his account of the child is about exposure:

The child later associates words with objects and activities, by implicit statistical inference ... At a later stage of linguistic development, similar statistical associations are developed between linguistic elements themselves. (p45, p46)
He has the right raw material, the statistics of which words occur with what, and he discusses predicting words from the preceding ones (p43, p54). He never proposes prediction as the thing to train on.

Words are known by the company they keep. Strong match, though not original to him.

The essential idea is that words can be seen to be associated not merely because they occur frequently together, but because they both occur frequently in conjunction with a third word (p71)
His example is that "ferry" and "fare" are related because both go with words like "bus". This is the basis of how modern systems represent word meaning. Linguists (Harris, Firth) had stated the idea in the 1950s. What Good adds is the argument that a machine needs it, since machines that "rely only on frequencies" (p71) can say nothing about combinations they haven't seen.

Word vectors. Partial match. On p52 and p53 he takes a table of how often each word occurs in each document, takes logarithms, subtracts a constant from each row and column, and proposes decomposing the result so that

This would associate a w-dimensional vector with each index term and with each document. The relevance of index term i to document j could now be defined as the correlation coefficient between the two associated vectors.
This is recognizably the method later known as latent semantic analysis (around 1990), and a relative of the word-embedding methods of the 2010s, which were shown to be doing something close to factoring a similar table. Two things are missing. He keeps as many dimensions as there are words, where the later methods get their power from keeping only a few hundred. And the vectors are computed once, not learned by a network. He also offers it only as "another conceivable method" and judges the computation "exceedingly great".

Generalization is the central problem. Strong match on the diagnosis, partial on the cure.

One of the main difficulties in this subject is how to estimate the probabilities of events that have never occurred. That such probabilities are relevant to intelligence is to be expected, since intelligence is sometimes defined as the ability to adapt to new circumstances. (p32)
This is still the right way to state it. Good had worked on this problem with Turing, and the resulting method (Good-Turing estimation) was a standard component of statistical language models into the 2000s. Current models don't use it. They generalize by learning that similar words and situations behave similarly, which is closer to his "ferry" and "fare" idea, and to his remark (p71) that getting the network to form abstractions is "one of the most vital problems".

What comes next depends on recent context and stored weights. Partial match. Good's unit of thought is the "assembly", Hebb's term for a group of neurons that fire together and stand for a word or idea.

Which assembly becomes active at the next moment must depend on the current sensory input, the current dominant assembly, and the currently active subassemblies. Indirectly, therefore, it depends on the recent assembly sequence, wherein the most recent assemblies will have the greatest influence. It also depends of course on the semipermanent static storage, the "past history." (p60)
A language model has the same division: what comes next is determined by the recent text it is looking at (its "context") and by weights fixed during training. Good's list of memory types (p72) puts short-term memory in current activity and long-term memory in connection strengths, which is the same split, and he says a long "attention span" is "certainly essential for intelligence" (p63). He goes on (p66) to score each candidate next assembly as a baseline plus a contribution from each recent one, with the highest total firing. The last step of a language model has that form, a score for every possible next word. But in a modern model the contributions from earlier words interact in complicated ways before that step, and Good only gestures at this by saying interaction terms will be needed (p67). I wouldn't claim more than a family resemblance.

Concepts are spread across many neurons. Strong match, shared credit.

each neuron would occur in a great many distinct circuits, and would not be indispensable for any of them. (p56)
He contrasts this with "one concept, one neuron". Modern networks store concepts as patterns over many units, with each unit taking part in many concepts, and this is a main reason their workings are hard to read off. The idea came from neuroscience (he cites Lashley and Eccles). Good's contribution is an efficiency argument for it, by analogy with a punched-card coding scheme.

Keep probabilities, not hard decisions. Strong match. Section 3 argues that a system understanding speech should pass along graded probabilities between its levels instead of committing to one answer at each, because "each definite 'decision' loses information" (p39). Modern networks pass continuous values between layers and only commit at the output.

Rejecting a logical "canonical language". Strong match. He considers representing meaning by translating every statement into a standard formal form, and concludes this would be "extremely difficult, perhaps even logically impossible, or perhaps it would require an ultraintelligent machine to do it!" (p41). Large projects later attempted roughly this and did not get far. Relatedly, his guess (p36, quoted in the main post) that natural language "rather than ... formal logic" is needed for scientific imagination is a partial match: current models do much of their reasoning by writing out steps in ordinary language.

Scale can substitute for design. Partial match.

a well-designed machine of say 109 components might be educable to ultraintelligence, but a much more carelessly designed machine of say 1013 components might be equally good. (p62)
The history of the field broadly supports this: simple methods given more computation have repeatedly beaten cleverer ones. But Good, following Ashby, bases it on the hope that almost any large, richly connected network will behave intelligently. That turned out to be false. Scale paid off only once there was a training method able to make use of it.

The hard part is ape-level intelligence. Partial match. He says "most of the struggle" will be building "a machine with the intelligence of an ape" (p45), because perception and basic learning are harder than what comes after. In favor: getting networks to learn to see took until about 2012, and fluent language followed within a decade. Against: language arrived without anything like an ape's physical competence, and robotics is still behind.

Sleep and replay. Partial match. His conjecture that sleep serves "to replay the assembly sequences that were of greatest interest during the day in order to consolidate them" (p80) is close to a well-supported view in neuroscience. In AI, replaying stored experience, with priority to the most informative parts, is a standard technique in systems that learn by trial and error. It is not part of how language models are mainly trained, so his suggestion that the machine would "benefit from periods of comparative rest" (p72) is a loose match at best.

Understanding as economy. Loose match. He argues that storing meanings instead of exact wordings saves a great deal of memory, and that this may be "the evolutionary function of meaning and understanding" (p77). There is a real modern parallel, since learning to predict text well and learning to compress it are mathematically the same task. Good's argument is about storage, though, and I think the connection is more suggestive than exact.

Hardware. Mixed. He was right that serial speed alone wouldn't do. He expected computers to become about a million times faster than neurons and still concluded the machine "will need to be ultraparallel" (p35), and current systems do depend on massively parallel chips. He was right that low power consumption "will be valuable" (p33). He was wrong that the neurons would be physical devices. They are simulated in software.

The brain as blueprint. Mostly a miss. The paper opens by saying that to design the machine "we need to understand more about the human brain or human thought or both", and later that brain anatomy is "very relevant" (p63). Current systems borrow the neuron and the adjustable connection and almost nothing else. Of the brain theory itself, Hebb's assemblies remain a respected idea in neuroscience, but the central control system Good relies on (taken from Penfield) has been abandoned, and his own extensions haven't been taken up. To his credit, he says the designer will have to guess which features of the brain matter, and he allows that the first machine might not use a neural network after all (p78).

Theory before experiment. Miss.

The need for further theory is great, since, without advances in theory, the amount of experimentation might be prohibitive. (p64)
Computation became cheap enough to experiment at enormous scale, and the systems we have were found that way. Theory explaining why they work is still well behind.

How much the machine needs to learn from. Miss. He sizes the machine's education to a person's: "A man cannot learn more than ten million statements in a lifetime" (p36). Current models learn much less from each example than people do, and compensate with volume. By my rough estimate they are trained on something like ten thousand times more text than a person could read in a lifetime.

Overall. Good was right about the kind of thing the machine would be: a very large, parallel neural network that learns the meanings of words from statistics, stores them as distributed patterns, treats generalization as the core problem, and works in natural language with conventional computers as tools. He was wrong, or silent, about how such a network could actually be trained, which is the part that took the field another fifty years. I'd put his reputation for foresight on these pages at least as much as on the famous paragraph.

[1] I generally see 1965, including on Wikipedia probably because of the publication date. But I think it's more informative to count by the date he wrote it: "The first draft of this monograph was completed in April 1963, and the present slightly amended version in May 1964."

item.title: Not just a bystander, not anymore…
item.description:
One Saturday night this summer, I was leisurely walking down main street hand-in-hand on a date, when suddenly, I heard a commotion about 50 yards down a busy side street. It was too far away to make out what was happening or what was being said. But I figured it was fine since the side street had plenty of people walking up and down it.

Still, I couldn’t help but peer into the distance, transfixed, like a deer in the headlights.

There was an anime convention going on that weekend. Initially, my brain reasoned that a couple of cosplayers were recording a TikTok video or doing a K-pop dance. Then my brain reasoned that surely, on a crowded street, nothing serious could be going down. Right?

Yet I waited there, unmoving, alert.

My date was casually standing there eating a cookie. She innocently asked, “What do you think’s going on over there?”

I faintly heard a woman yelling. While squinting, I saw sudden, physical contact between her and a man. I dropped my date’s hand and began aggressively stomping towards them. 

All I could see was red.

I used to have anger problems during my adolescence. I didn't realize that maybe I was different from other people, until one day during my freshman year of college…
 

…I opened the door to my apartment to find a roomful of friends. One of them stood up from the couch to give me a hug with her arms outstretched, one hand high and the other hand low. I instinctually flinched, and then leaned in to give her a hug, but she pulled back and stopped. 

“I noticed that you always flinch before I give you a hug,” she said. “How come?”

I thought about it for a second, then copied her—one hand high and the other low—then nonchalantly said, “Your high hand? That’s probably the angle from which my dad hits me.”

Her face dropped. I looked around. Everyone else’s side conversations had stopped and they were all staring at me. I noticed that I was confused—did I say something weird? My friend had asked me a question and I had matter-of-factly gave the answer. I had no idea why everyone was being so weird. I inquired, “What?”

My friend, the one who got up to give me a hug, looked at me sympathetically. “Your dad hits you?”

I noticed that I was confused again. They care about that? I gestured to the group of wide-eyed people and asserted, “What, your dads never hit you?”

Everyone stayed frozen. Then my roommate on the couch softly said, “No dude. My dad’s never hit me.” Slowly, others nodded their heads in agreement.

I felt a note of disgust. I didn’t need their pity. I retorted, “My dad’s not a monster. He doesn’t just randomly hit me for no reason. Only if I do something stupid or disobey him.” Feeling satisfied at successfully defending my dad and at clearing up the matter, my satisfaction turned into an admixture of confusion and anger—they were still just staring at me in stunned silence and pity.

“Whatever.” I went into my room and shut the door.

He was kicking her. The man was kicking her. As I stomped closer to them, my anger continued to build into a white-hot fury. My fury was only slightly abated by a thought that confused me: it’s a crowded street, there’s even a group of dads walking by and laughing with each other, so why is no one doing anything? Never mind that. My anger was building into an unstoppable rage.

Thirty feet from the assaulter, I did something that I haven’t done since I was a child—I screamed at the top of my lungs:

“HEYYY!!!”

The attacker whipped his head towards me in confused fear. I stormed forward and screamed:

“GET THE FUCK AWAY FROM HER.”

I must have had the twisted face of a rabid dog; the whites of the man’s eyes shined like saucers.

The woman screamed, “He’s trying to rape me!”

After that day in college, I reflected on my friends' reactions. Really? Their dads never hit them? Then how did their dads maintain their authority if not through fear? I couldn’t fathom an alternative method. So I shrugged and wrote them off as probably being weak.

Going forward, not much changed. I continued to exert my will over my four college roommates through intimidation and by yelling at them. Throughout my freshman year of college, one-by-one, my friends stopped coming by my apartment to say hi, stopped returning my texts, and were increasingly "too busy" to hang out when I ran into them on campus. I never felt lonely. No, I was too prideful for that. All these people just sucked. I just needed to find new, better friends. But new people, for whatever reason, didn’t stick around for too long.

This went on into my sophomore year of college. It went on until the day I had a bad trip while taking psychedelic mushrooms…
 

…So there I was, sitting on the ground of my university squash court with my friend, and beginning to hallucinate. At first, the spotted wood of the court looked like ants marching towards me, which was amusing.

It was amusing until, suddenly, a demon materialized in my stomach, crawled up my spinal cord, and invaded my mind. The most violent, envious, prideful thoughts spewed out of me. While it was happening, I believed it was the demon saying these things, not me, therefore not my responsibility and not my problem.

The next day, however, I realized that the demon was a manifestation of my innermost insecurities. That what the demon spake wasn’t gibberish nonsense, but instead a prophecy of what was to come if I didn’t get my shit together.

That experience scared me straight. And ever since that day seven years ago, I’m very proud that I never lost control again. I never yelled at anyone ever again. Until…

The man ignored me and started kicking her again.

Incensed, I advanced towards him and roared even louder, “HEY! GET THE FUCK AWAY FROM HER.” The man saw me stomping towards him and he stuttered backwards. Perhaps he saw in my eyes that I wasn’t fucking around, that I wanted blood.

They say that in response to immense stress, people typically have one of three reactions: fight, flight, or freeze. I was ready to fight. But it hasn’t always been like this…

As a child, I sometimes found myself on the other side of the kitchen table, playing a game of cat & mouse with my angry older brother, tears and snot streaming down my face, squealing like a cornered pig about to be slaughtered, while trying to avoid my brother’s grasp. For I knew if he caught me, he would wrestle me to the floor, pin my arms underneath him by sitting on my torso, and then rain blows down upon me.

Over the years, after repeatedly being hit by my father, by my mother, and by my brother, I learned that flight was not a good strategy for me. I was the youngest and the weakest. I was never going to be able to outrun them or outfight them. Instead, I figured out that it was far better to freeze, study what triggered them, and then learn to tiptoe around those landmines. 

And this worked. I learned to suppress my emotions while living with my family. It was the only way to assure my safety.

When I moved away to college, I turned into a monster. All my pent-up anger was unleashed upon my innocent roommates and friends. And it felt good. Fuck, it felt so good to lean in to my newfound rage. I got to feel powerful for once. I got to feel in control. And it worked…until it didn’t. One-by-one my friends left me.

 

After the psychedelic trip, I underwent a years-long healing journey. I read dozens of EQ, therapy, and self-help books. I wrote thousands of pages across my journals. I laughed, I cried, I got in touch with my emotions that I had suppressed my whole life. And then I decided to get strong.

In the latter half of college, "The House of Iron" became my place of worship—every day I was in the gym at 6am for two hours. In the span of ten months, I went from barely being able to lift a barbell, to deadlifting twice my body weight. I put on 10-15lbs of muscle, and when I looked in the mirror, instead of seeing a scared kid, for the first time in my life I saw the body of a man looking back.

 

The last time my whole family lived under the same roof was my senior year of college. My brother and I had been getting along for a while, becoming friends for the first time in our lives. I thought there was mutual respect between us. 

I was wrong.

One morning the dog ran down the hallway loudly, and in the process, accidentally woke up my brother. Watching it happen, I began chuckling at the ridiculousness of it. My brother burst out of his room and saw me quietly snickering. He assumed that I had deliberately woken him up to mess with him, and without asking questions, sprinted towards me and unleashed a barrage of punches. I froze. 

Then after a moment, I realized that his punches didn’t hurt. Not anymore. I had gotten stronger since the last time he struck me. 

He kept hitting me and accusing me, “You woke me up! You woke me up!” I grabbed both of his arms, stopping the assault, and told him, “It was the dog! It was the dog! The dog accidentally woke you up, not me!” He stopped thrashing, stared at me with suspicion, then shrugged and went into the kitchen to go make coffee.

I just stood there, stunned. Then I went into my room and closed the door. Five minutes later I joined my first Zoom class for the day. During that call, I silently processed what had just happened. I felt confused, shocked, angry.

After my class, I went looking for my brother, and found him in the backyard by the pool on a lounge chair sunbathing in nothing but his boxers, peacefully reading a book.

“Hey,” I called to him.

He casually turned his head towards me.

“Like I said this morning,” I stated in a cool, even tone while maintaining intense, unblinking eye contact. “It was the dog that woke you up, not me. And without thinking or asking clarifying questions, you attacked me. Look at me,” I demanded while pointing at my eyes. “I’m bigger than you now. I’m stronger than you now. And if you ever put hands on me again, I will fuck you up. There will be blood.” 

He looked at me and saw that I wasn’t fucking around. I dialed my intensity down, smiled, and then told him, “have a nice day.”

I wasn’t a bystander, not anymore.

The man was conflicted. He wanted to continue kicking this woman, but he also saw the bloodlust in my eyes. He tried reasoning with me:

“She pepper-sprayed me!”

“I don’t give a FUCK,” I replied. “Get the FUCK away from her.” 

The man teetered on his backfoot, unsure of what to do. And while he was doing that, I was mentally preparing how I was going to incapacitate him.

Had my half-naked sunbathing brother actually gotten up to fight, it would have been ugly. Neither of us are trained fighters. But ultimately, the threat of me fighting back for the first time was enough to deter all future conflicts. He gained a kind of respect for me that day. While we've had our ups and downs in the years since then, today we’ve never been closer as brothers. He's a good guy.

But had we fought that day, it would have been a mess of sprawling limbs. But that wouldn’t be the case today because…
 

…Last year I made a new friend at a coffee shop—an older gentleman. What an amazing and wise individual. In his youth, he was a hothead like me, and he also grew up with a brother that beat him.

But unlike me, as a young adult he got into dozens of street fights and learned how to defend himself through trial by fire.

One day, months into our friendship, he asked me, “Do you want to learn how to fight?”

“Yes.”

And thus began my training.

 

Punches. Kicks. Blocks. And also the psychology of fighting—people, especially untrained fighters, are predictable. The most common punch thrown from the untrained fighter is the overhead haymaker. My friend taught me how to block that—turns out that the wax on/wax off technique from Karate Kid actually works—and then how to counter with a series of devastating blows. 

An older man who instills wisdom, philosophy, and the means to defend myself. I had met my Mr. Miyagi.

At my gym, I began using a punching bag without any gloves to toughen my hands. The first time I did bag work, I whiffed a roundhouse kick and landed hard on my ass. I also walked away with nasty bruises up and down my shins, arms, and fingers. 

But over time I got tougher. When I would visit my friend, he would surprise attack me to try to catch me off guard. And gradually, my reaction time got better.

Over the course of a few months, I developed a newfound confidence when walking around downtown. It felt like I was armed. And I was. My body became acutely primed to defend itself. I was now ready if a fight ever went down…

When he charges, I thought, I’ll block the first punch, and counter with an elbow strike to his ear with all my force to go for a knockout blow.

I took a step forward, my eyes subconsciously communicating: please, enter the arena.

The man took a step back, scowled, and slinked away from the woman he was attacking.

I followed him.

I lived with my parents for a few years after college to save money. Before I moved out, I had one goal.

After dinner one night, I announced to my parents, “I’m pretty emotionally fucked up. And so are both of you. I’m going to singlehandedly carry this family’s trauma and stress on my back until we’re all healed.” They mocked me for making such a grandiose declaration, but I didn’t care. I didn’t know how I was going to fix us, but I was fully resolved in my ability to do so.

As I read more books and had emotionally challenging conversations with friends, I took what I learned and practiced at home. One night in particular stood out to me.

I don’t remember what they were arguing about, but it didn’t matter. What mattered was that my father was yelling at my mother. And I was fucking pissed about it.

“HEY,” I exclaimed.

My parents looked at me, probably expecting me to complain about the noise they were making when I was trying to work. Instead, I furiously pointed an accusatory finger at my father and loudly asserted, “You’re not going to yell at my mother again.”

My father looked at me with a blank expression.
 

We all just stood there in silence.
 

I narrowed my eyes. “Got it?”

My father, not breaking eye contact with me, said “yeah” then walked away.

Had my father—who is bigger, taller, and stronger—challenged me and tried to intimidate me, I would have had no choice but to back down. Maybe he saw the resolve in my eyes, and in a moment of self-reflection, realized how he was treating his wife. In that moment, perhaps he overcame the rough childhood he endured and chose peace.

I wish I could say that everything immediately got better after that night. But it didn’t. Lots of hard conversations ensued over that year. Tears were shed. Yelling.

I made plenty of mistakes, too, allowing my ego to get the better of me. The road was rocky, but I ultimately kept my promise: I carried my family out of the dregs of our emotional abyss by repeatedly modeling good behavior, choosing the right time to initiate difficult conversations, and believing that I could even do this in the first place.

Today, my parents and I have never been closer. I’m proud of them, and my brother. They all put the work in to become better versions of themselves, and they deserve the credit for that. They're not perfect (far from it), but they've come a long way.

It’s been seven years since the last time I lost control, when the psychedelic demon took over my mind. And now I’m following an attacker.

The man, sporting the craziest of eyes, was huffing and puffing, “She started it! That crazy bitch pepper-sprayed me!”

“FUCK off,” I fumed.

The man walked alongside the group of dads I’d passed earlier and tried to fraternize with them, “That bitch is crazy! Did you see that?? She’s crazy!” The dad closest to him nodded sympathetically with a half-smile to appease him.

I continued following the man up the street. Any time he turned around to gripe about the woman, I shouted, “FUCK off.” We got to the next street intersection and I watched him walk away while muttering to himself. 

I wasn’t a bystander, not anymore.

 

When he got a far enough distance away and appeared to not be returning, I remembered what I was doing that night—I was on a date.

I turned around. My date was watching me. She was eating a cookie.

Weeks later, I sat down to write this story alone in my apartment. Remembering everything that happened that day, I began to relive the experience. My heart started beating out of my chest, I broke into a sweat. I felt so, so fucking angry.

What I still didn’t understand was: on a crowded street, a man was openly assaulting a woman, yet people just watched and moved along—why did no one else help? While writing this story, I sat back in my chair and stared out the window, waiting for the answer to come to me. 

And then it did.

 

 

The man, and the woman he was attacking, were both homeless.

 

 

It’s been over two years since I last cried. 

Sitting at my desk thinking about all this, overwhelmed with emotion, I began to open-mouth weep. I covered my face in shame (because men aren’t supposed to cry), I recognized how silly this was given that I was alone in my apartment, gargled a wet laugh at the irony, then I wept.

I was thinking of Teresa.

 

 

Part 1: I would have shit in that alley, too
Part 2: A City Within a City
Part 3: Assaulted
Final Part: Not just a bystander, not anymore…
